narrative:
The model estimated a 58.9% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is a more-likely-than-not risk, and it is why your law school application was rejected: the admissions decision treated this predicted bar-exam risk as too high to approve.

The strongest factor driving that prediction was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That large gap was the most influential reason the model leaned toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year standing also pushed the prediction toward failure: you were in the third decile, compared with an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, though this mattered less than your third-year standing. By contrast, your LSAT score of 38 was slightly above the accepted-student average of about 37, and it was the main factor pushing toward a prediction of passing. It was not strong enough to outweigh the concerns raised by your class standing. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To move forward, ask admissions for a human review and explain any circumstances behind your grades. Focus on strengthening your academic record, especially upper-level performance, and consider retaking the LSAT only if practice results show a meaningful gain. Meet with a pre-law advisor, build a clear remediation plan, and reapply once you can show stronger evidence of bar-exam readiness.
